title: C-RADIOv4: A Distilled Vision Foundation Model for FiftyOne
author: Harpreet Sahota
summary: Introduction The field of computer vision has seen remarkable progress with vision foundation models that excel at specific tasks—CLIP for vision-language alignment, DINOv3 for dense perception, SAM3 for segmentation . But what if you could distill the best of these foundation models into a single, unified architecture? That's exactly what C-RADIOv4 achieves. C-RADIOv4 is the latest release in NVIDIA Labs' agglomerative vision foundation model family. Through innovative multi-teacher distillation, it creates a unified student model that retains and improves upon the distinct capabilities of multiple state-of-the-art teachers: SigLIP2 , DINOv3 , and SAM3 . In this blog post, we'll explore what makes C-RADIOv4 special, dive into its technical innovations, and show you how to leverage its powerful capabilities in FiftyOne for computer vision workflows . What are foundation models? Foundation models are large, pretrained models that learn broad, reusable representations from massive datasets and can be adapted to many downstream tasks with little or no task-specific training. What is C-RADIOv4? C-RADIOv4 is an agglomerative foundation model that learns from multiple teacher models simultaneously. Instead of training on labeled data, it distills foundation model knowledge from three cutting-edge vision models: SigLIP2: The frontier text-image foundation encoder, providing enhanced zero-shot classification capabilities DINOv3 : A self-supervised learning powerhouse that delivers strong dense perception and semantic segmentation SAM3 : The latest iteration of Segment Anything Model, enabling powerful segmentation capabilities The result? A single vision language model that combines text-image alignment, dense perception, and segmentation—all while maintaining competitive performance at a fraction of the parameters of its teachers. Get started with C-RADIOv4 → C-RADIOv4: Vision foundation model variants C-RADIOv4 comes in two variants: Both foundation models achieve impressive results: Zero-shot accuracy : 83.09% (H) and 82.01% (SO400M) on ImageNet-1K kNN accuracy : 86.59% (H) and 85.76% (SO400M) on ImageNet-1K Semantic segmentation : 55.20 mIoU (H) and 55.14 mIoU (SO400M) on ADE20k Remarkably, C-RADIOv4-H achieves performance competitive with DINOv3-7B (which has 6.7B parameters) on dense tasks, despite having an order of magnitude fewer parameters. C-RADIOv4: Key technical innovations for vision foundation models 1. Stochastic resolution training Previous RADIO vision foundation models trained at just two resolutions, which could lead to inconsistent behavior at inference time—a phenomenon called "mode switching." C-RADIOv4 solves this by training across a wide range of resolutions: Low-resolution partition : {128, 192, 224, 256, 384, 432} pixels High-resolution partition : {512, 768, 1024, 1152} pixels This enables smooth resolution scaling and substantial quality improvements at low resolutions. The model demonstrates strong robustness even at resolutions higher than those it was trained on, achieving 57.72 mIoU at 1536px on ADE20k. 2. Shift equivariance One challenge in foundation model distillation is that students can learn not just useful features, but also fixed-pattern noise from teachers. C-RADIOv4 addresses this with two forms of shift equivariance: Shift Equivariant Loss : Randomly shifts crops for both student and teachers independently, preventing the model from learning position-dependent artifacts Shift Equivariant MESA : Applies exponential moving average matching with different crops, further reducing fixed-pattern noise These techniques ensure the model learns robust, semantically meaningful features rather than spurious patterns. 3. ViTDet mode for high-resolution efficiency For high-resolution inference, C-RADIOv4 supports "ViTDet mode," which uses windowed attention instead of full global attention. This dramatically reduces inference time: The SO400M variant with ViTDet window size ≤ 12 is faster than SAM3's encoder ViT-H with window size 8 is nearly as fast as SAM3 Latency scales much more favorably with resolution compared to full attention This makes C-RADIOv4 practical for real-world applications requiring high-resolution processing. 4. Balanced summary loss Different teachers produce summary features with different angular dispersions. Without normalization, teachers with larger dispersion would dominate the loss. C-RADIOv4 uses an angular loss formulation that normalizes for each teacher's cone radius, ensuring balanced learning from all teachers. Getting started with C-RADIOv4 in FiftyOne FiftyOne provides seamless integration with C-RADIOv4, making it easy to leverage these powerful capabilities in your computer vision workflows . Installation First, install FiftyOne and register the C-RADIOv4 model source: # Install FiftyOne pip install fiftyone # Register the RADIO model source import fiftyone.zoo as foz foz . register_zoo_model_source ( " https://github.com/harpreetsahota204/CRADIOv4 " , ) Quick start: Computing embeddings The most common use case is extracting image embeddings for similarity search, clustering, and visualization: import fiftyone as fo import fiftyone.zoo as foz # Load your dataset dataset = foz . load_zoo_dataset ( " quickstart " , shuffle = True ) # Load the C-RADIOv4 model model = foz . load_zoo_model ( " nv_labs/c-radio_v4-h " ) # Compute embeddings with efficient batching dataset . compute_embeddings ( model = model , embeddings_field = " radio_embeddings " , batch_size = 16 , # Adjust based on GPU memory num_workers = 4 # Parallel data loading ) # Launch the FiftyOne App to explore session = fo . launch_app ( dataset ) Model configuration options C-RADIOv4 offers flexible configuration for different use cases: # Global image embeddings (default) model = foz . load_zoo_model ( " nv_labs/c-radio_v4-h " , output_type = " summary " , # Global semantic features feature_format = " NCHW " # or "NLC" ) # Spatial attention features spatial_model = foz . load_zoo_model ( " nv_labs/c-radio_v4-h " , output_type = " spatial " , # Patch-level spatial features feature_format = " NCHW " , # Required for spatial apply_smoothing = True , # Gaussian smoothing for cleaner heatmaps smoothing_sigma = 1.51 # Smoothing strength ) C-RADIOv4: Practical use cases for vision foundation models 1. Embedding visualization with UMAP Create beautiful 2D visualizations of your image embeddings to understand dataset structure: import fiftyone.brain as fob # Compute embeddings first dataset . compute_embeddings ( model = model , embeddings_field = " radio_embeddings " ) # Create UMAP visualization results = fob . compute_visualization ( dataset , method = " umap " , # Also supports "tsne", "pca" brain_key = " radio_viz " , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " ) # Explore in the App session = fo . launch_app ( dataset ) The visualization reveals clusters of similar images, making it easy to identify patterns and outliers in your dataset. 2. Similarity search Build powerful similarity search capabilities: import fiftyone.brain as fob # Build similarity index results = fob . compute_similarity ( dataset , backend = " sklearn " , brain_key = " radio_sim " , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " ) # Find similar images sample_id = dataset . first (). id similar_samples = dataset . sort_by_similarity ( sample_id , brain_key = " radio_sim " , k = 10 # Top 10 most similar ) # View results session = fo . launch_app ( similar_samples ) This is incredibly useful for: Finding duplicate or near-duplicate images Discovering similar content for data augmentation Building recommendation systems Quality control and anomaly detection 3. Spatial attention heatmaps Visualize what regions of an image the model focuses on using spatial attention features: # Load spatial model with smoothing spatial_model = foz . load_zoo_model ( " nv_labs/c-radio_v4-h " , output_type = " spatial " , apply_smoothing = True , smoothing_sigma = 1.51 , feature_format = " NCHW " ) # Generate attention heatmaps dataset . apply_model ( spatial_model , " radio_heatmap " , batch_size = 16 , num_workers = 4 ) # View heatmaps in FiftyOne App session = fo . launch_app ( dataset ) The heatmaps use PCA visualization (as described in the C-RADIOv4 paper) to show object boundaries and regions of interest. This is particularly useful for: Understanding model behavior Debugging and interpretability Identifying important image regions Quality assessment 4. Dataset curation: Uniqueness and representativeness Use embeddings to score how unique or representative each sample is: import fiftyone.brain as fob # Compute uniqueness scores fob . compute_uniqueness ( dataset , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " ) # Compute representativeness scores fob . compute_representativeness ( dataset , representativeness_field = " radio_represent " , method = " cluster-center " , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " ) # Find most representative samples representative_view = dataset . sort_by ( " radio_represent " , reverse = True ) These scores help with: Active learning : Select diverse samples for labeling Dataset balancing : Identify underrepresented regions Data cleaning : Find outliers and edge cases Efficient annotation : Prioritize representative samples 5. Duplicate detection Automatically find and remove near-duplicate images: import fiftyone.brain as fob # Detect duplicates using embeddings results = fob . compute_uniqueness ( dataset , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " ) # Filter to most unique samples unique_view = dataset . sort_by ( " uniqueness " , reverse = True ) This is essential for: Cleaning datasets before training Reducing storage costs Improving dataset quality Preventing data leakage in train/test splits Advanced workflows for vision foundation models Comprehensive analysis pipeline Combine multiple C-RADIOv4 outputs for thorough dataset analysis: # Step 1: Global embeddings for similarity embedding_model = foz . load_zoo_model ( " nv_labs/c-radio_v4-h " ) dataset . compute_embeddings ( embedding_model , " radio_embeddings " ) # Step 2: Spatial heatmaps for attention analysis spatial_model = foz . load_zoo_model ( " nv_labs/c-radio_v4-h " , output_type = " spatial " , apply_smoothing = True , smoothing_sigma = 0.8 ) dataset . apply_model ( spatial_model , " radio_heatmap " ) # Step 3: Build similarity index import fiftyone.brain as fob fob . compute_similarity ( dataset , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " , brain_key = " radio_sim " ) # Step 4: Compute additional metrics fob . compute_uniqueness ( dataset , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " ) fob . compute_representativeness ( dataset , embeddings = " radio_embeddings " ) # Step 5: Comprehensive exploration session = fo . launch_app ( dataset ) This pipeline gives you: Similarity search for finding related images Attention visualization for understanding model focus Uniqueness scores for identifying outliers Representativeness scores for dataset balancing Interactive exploration in the FiftyOne App Performance optimization for vision foundation models Batch processing For optimal performance on large datasets, use batching with parallel data loading: dataset . compute_embeddings ( model = model , embeddings_field = " radio_embeddings " , batch_size = 16 , # Adjust based on GPU memory num_workers = 4 # Parallel data loading workers ) Recommended batch sizes by GPU: RTX 3090/4090 (24GB): batch_size=16-32 A100 (40GB/80GB): batch_size=32-64 Smaller GPUs: batch_size=4-8 GPU acceleration C-RADIOv4 automatically uses GPU acceleration with mixed precision (bfloat16) on compatible hardware (Ampere+). The vision foundation model automatically handles: Device placement (GPU/CPU) Mixed precision inference Efficient memory management High-resolution processing For high-resolution images, consider using the SO400M variant with ViTDet mode enabled (when available through the API) for faster inference: # Use smaller model for faster inference model = foz . load_zoo_model ( " nv_labs/c-radio_v4-so400m " ) Real-world applications for vision foundation models C-RADIOv4 has been successfully deployed in various domains: Autonomous Vehicles : Dense perception for scene understanding Robotics : Visual navigation and manipulation Document Processing : OCR and document parsing (Nemotron Parse) Open Vocabulary Segmentation : RADSeg uses RADIO for state-of-the-art segmentation Vision-Language Models : Used as vision encoder in Nemotron Nano V2 VL The vision foundation model's permissive license (NVIDIA Open Model License Agreement) makes it suitable for both research and commercial applications. Why C-RADIOv4? Unified capabilities Instead of maintaining separate models for different tasks, C-RADIOv4 provides: Zero-shot classification (from SigLIP2) Dense perception (from DINOv3) Segmentation capabilities (from SAM3) All in a single, efficient model. Efficiency With 631M parameters (H variant) or 412M parameters (SO400M variant), C-RADIOv4 achieves performance competitive with models having 10x more parameters, making it practical for deployment. Flexibility Works across a wide range of resolutions (128px to 1152px+) Supports both global embeddings and spatial features Can replace SAM3's vision encoder for segmentation tasks ViTDet mode enables efficient high-resolution processing Quality The vision foundation model demonstrates: Cleaner object boundaries (as shown in PCA visualizations) Strong resolution scaling properties Robust performance across diverse benchmarks Reduced fixed-pattern noise compared to individual teachers Foundation model distillation and the road ahead for vision models C-RADIOv4 represents a significant advancement in agglomerative vision foundation models. By combining the strengths of SigLIP2, DINOv3, and SAM3 through innovative foundation model distillation techniques, it delivers a unified model that's both powerful and efficient. The integration with FiftyOne makes it easy to leverage these capabilities for: Dataset exploration and visualization Similarity search and duplicate detection Attention visualization and interpretability Dataset curation and active learning Quality control and anomaly detection Whether you're working on autonomous vehicles, robotics , document processing, or any computer vision application, C-RADIOv4 provides a solid foundation for your workflows. title: GridSearchCV in scikit-learn
author: MedVall
summary: What is GridSearchCV ? GridSearchCV is a tool in Scikit-learn that finds the best hyperparameters for a machine learning model by testing different combinations. GridSearchCV stands for Grid Search with Cross-Validation. How does it work ? It tests combinations of hyperparameters using cross-validation, splits the training data into multiple folds, and compares the average performance. Finally, it selects the combination that achieves the best cross-validation score. How to use it ? Define a model, create a parameter grid, and pass both to GridSearchCV Why is it important in model training ? GridSearchCV helps improve model performance by finding suitable hyperparameters and reduces the risk of choosing settings based on a single validation split. It can improve generalization, but it does not guarantee better results on unseen data. Important attributes best_params_: the best hyperparameter combination found. best_score_: the best mean cross-validation score. best_estimator_: the model trained with the best parameters. cv_results_: detailed results for all tested combinations. Conclusion GridSearchCV automates hyperparameter tuning and helps you select a well-performing machine learning model.

title: How I caught a crash by actually running someone's fix
author: CH
summary: Most code review on open source PRs is reading. Someone looks at the diff, it makes sense, they leave a thumbs up. I've started doing something a bit different: I actually install the PR and run it. On Windows, which turns out to be the part that matters. Today I tried it on three open PRs in simonw/llm , the command-line tool for talking to language models. Here's what happened. PR 1: a clean exit that crashed on start This PR made llm chat exit cleanly when you hit end-of-input, instead of printing "Aborted!". The diff was small and looked fine. But it called click.termui._readline_prompt , a private function inside the click library. That function only exists in click 8.4 and newer, and llm doesn't pin a click version. So I set up a throwaway venv and ran it three ways: main: "Aborted!" (the original bug) the PR with click 8.5: clean exit, works the PR with click 8.3.1: AttributeError the moment chat starts So the fix works on the newest click and breaks chat completely on anything older. Reading the diff, you'd never see that. I posted the results and suggested either pinning click>=8.4 or catching EOFError around a plain input() . PR 2: a Windows fix that still fails on Windows This one was about llm install / llm uninstall , running pip in a separate process so llm can update itself. On Windows I ran the self-reinstall case on main and on the PR. main: pip refuses to modify itself the PR: WinError 5 (access denied) on a .pyd file The running llm process has that compiled extension loaded, and Windows locks loaded files, so the child pip can't replace it. Different error, same result: it still can't reinstall itself while running. Again, nothing in the diff tells you that. You have to run it on Windows. PR 3: a cleanup that was just fine The third PR removed some old Windows-only readline setup lines. The author said they couldn't reproduce the original problem, so nobody was sure it was safe. I ran it on main and on the PR, checked that chat opens and arrow keys still work, and both behaved the same. So I left a short "tested on Windows, looks good as a cleanup". Not every test finds a bug, and a confirmed "it's fine" is useful too. What I took from it Running a PR takes maybe 15 minutes with a throwaway venv. That's often more than the author could do, because they might not have your OS or your versions. Private functions and unpinned dependencies are where "works on my machine" hides. Try the oldest version the project allows, not just the newest. Windows is underrepresented among testers. If you're on Windows, you're already useful. Post exactly what you ran and what happened. Let the maintainer decide what to do with it. Disclosure: I used AI (Claude) to help pick PRs, write the little test scripts, and draft this post. I ran every test myself on my own PC, and the results above are what I saw.

title: GSTR-2B Reconciliation Made Simple
author: Subhendu Das
summary: The Challenge of Manual Reconciliation For Indian SMBs, reconciling the purchase register against the GSTR‑2B feed is a monthly chore that involves thousands of invoice line items. Each line must be matched by vendor, GSTIN, invoice number, amount, tax rate, and HSN code. The current manual workflow relies on spreadsheets, ad‑hoc filters, and a lot of trial‑and‑error. Even a single misplaced comma can trigger a cascade of “unmatched” flags, forcing finance teams to dig through logs and re‑enter data. This is where gst reconciliation software pays off in practice. GSTBot’s Reconciliation Engine GSTBot replaces that pain with an automated, tolerance‑aware engine. The core of the engine is a FastAPI endpoint that accepts a batch of PDFs, photos, or Excel files, forwards them to a Celery worker, and stores the parsed data in PostgreSQL. The worker then performs a fuzzy join against the GSTR‑2B download, using a configurable tolerance window for numeric fields. # FastAPI route that triggers the reconciliation @router.post ( " /reconcile " ) async def reconcile_invoices ( file : UploadFile = File (...)): task_id = await celery_app . send_task ( " tasks.reconcile " , args = [ file . filename ]) return { " task_id " : task_id } The Celery task pulls the file from S3, runs the AI extraction model, and writes the results to a parsed_invoices table. @celery_app.task ( name = " tasks.reconcile " ) def reconcile ( file_name : str ): invoices = extract_invoices ( file_name ) # AI extraction session . execute ( insert ( parsed_invoices ). values ( invoices )) session . commit () perform_match () The perform_match function performs the heart of the reconciliation: Getting gst reconciliation software right early saves rework later. # PostgreSQL query that joins parsed invoices with GSTR‑2B entries query = ( select ( pi . id . label ( " invoice_id " ), gb . id . label ( " gstr_id " ), abs ( pi . amount - gb . amount ). label ( " amount_diff " ) ) . select_from ( parsed_invoices . alias ( " pi " )) . join ( gstr2b . alias ( " gb " ), and_ ( pi . vendor == gb . vendor , pi . gstin == gb . gstin , pi . invoice_no == gb . invoice_no , func . abs ( pi . amount - gb . amount ) <= 0.01 * pi . amount )) ) results = session . execute ( query ). fetchall () The tolerance of 1 % is configurable via the settings.py module. If an amount differs by more than the threshold, the engine flags the line as an exception and stores it in an exceptions table for later review. How the Engine Works Ingestion – Users upload bulk invoice files through the React UI. The front‑end calls the /reconcile endpoint and receives a task ID. Extraction – A Celery worker runs the open‑source OCR and NLP pipeline to pull vendor name, GSTIN, invoice number, amount, tax rate, and HSN code. The extraction results are written to PostgreSQL. Matching – A Postgres query joins the parsed invoices with the GSTR‑2B dataset, applying a 1 % tolerance on amounts. The query uses func.abs to compute the absolute difference. Exception Classification – Any unmatched rows are routed through a rule engine that tags the exception (e.g., missing vendor , amount mismatch , HSN mismatch ) and suggests a corrective action. Reporting – The results are surfaced in the UI as a drill‑down table. Finance staff can approve, edit, or flag each exception, and the changes propagate back to the parsed_invoices table. The entire flow is orchestrated by Redis, which holds the Celery task queue. Redis is configured with a short TTL (5 min) so that stalled tasks are automatically retried. The health endpoint ( /health/jobs ) reports the status of the broker, ensuring that the system is always aware of queue back‑pressure. Example Flow A small manufacturer uploads a 50‑page PDF of purchase invoices. The React UI shows a progress bar as the file is uploaded. Once the Celery task starts, the AI extraction takes 12 seconds per page, a 30 % improvement over the legacy OCR tool. The matching query runs in 0.8 seconds, producing 47 matches and 3 exceptions. The UI lists the exceptions with a color‑coded status and a one‑click “Edit” button. Good gst reconciliation software keeps the rest of the workflow predictable. { "exceptions" : [ { "invoice_id" : 1023 , "reason" : "amount mismatch" , "suggested_action" : "re‑enter amount" }, { "invoice_id" : 1047 , "reason" : "missing vendor" , "suggested_action" : "add vendor" } ] } Finance staff can resolve the two exceptions in under a minute, after which the system automatically updates the input tax credit (ITC) ledger. The reconciled data feeds directly into the GSTR‑1 and GSTR‑3B generation modules, completing the compliance cycle. Technical Highlights FastAPI handles the HTTP layer and provides a lightweight, async API. Celery + Redis decouples heavy extraction and matching logic from the request cycle, enabling horizontal scaling. PostgreSQL stores parsed invoices and GSTR‑2B data; its jsonb column stores raw OCR output for audit trails. Configurable Tolerances are exposed via environment variables, allowing a 0.5 % or 2 % threshold depending on business rules. Robust Error Handling – When the Redis broker is unreachable, the worker logs a 503 with Retry-After instead of a 500, and the UI displays a friendly message. Security – OAuth providers that redirect to localhost are blocked, and Microsoft’s email_verified claim is enforced to prevent spoofed sign‑ins. GSTBot’s reconciliation engine exemplifies how a focused, well‑structured stack can transform a manual, error‑prone task into a repeatable, auditable workflow. By leveraging FastAPI, Celery, Redis, and PostgreSQL, the system delivers accurate, tolerance‑aware ITC reconciliation for Indian SMBs, eliminating the need for spreadsheets and reducing month‑end cycle time. title: Why I love building 100% client-side web tools (and how I do it)
author: huali
summary: I'm a solo indie developer based in China. Over the past year I've built more than 20 small web tools, and almost all of them share one design decision: no backend at all. Here's why I keep coming back to it. No server means no data risk. When a tool runs entirely in the browser, the user's input never leaves their device. There's no database to leak, no logs to inspect, no "we may share data with partners" paragraph to write. Privacy stops being a policy and becomes an architecture. For things like a BMI calculator or a password generator, that's the right default. Instant load. A single HTML file with inline CSS and JS is a few kilobytes. It renders before a typical React app has finished downloading its framework. Fast tools feel trustworthy. Near-zero cost. Static files on Cloudflare Pages cost me basically nothing. No servers to patch, no uptime alerts at 3 a.m., no scaling bill when a post goes viral. How I actually build them: plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. No build step, no framework. I deploy to Cloudflare Pages with a git push. I use AI as a pair programmer — mostly for scaffolding layouts and catching edge cases — but I keep the logic simple enough to read in one sitting. That stack is what powers Lihayo Tools, a growing set of 20+ free utilities including BMI and TDEE calculators. Everything runs locally, no signup, no tracking. If you've been thinking about shipping small tools, start with a single HTML file. It's still the most underrated stack on the web.

title: Running SEO Checks in a CI Pipeline: What to Automate
author: Jay Barker
summary:
The deploy went green. Every test passed. Two days later, someone in marketing posted a Search Console screenshot in Slack: pages were dropping out of the index. A template change had shipped a noindex tag that was only ever meant for staging. Nothing in the pipeline caught it, because nothing in the pipeline was looking. Unit tests check that your code behaves. They don't check the HTML that Googlebot actually receives. This post is a practical plan for running SEO checks in a CI pipeline. It covers which checks to automate, where each one should run, and which ones to leave to humans. Every script below was tested before publishing, and you can drop them into a GitHub Actions setup today. If you've wanted to start automated SEO testing but weren't sure where the line was, this is it. Why SEO Breaks Quietly in Deploys SEO regressions are sneaky because nothing errors out. The page loads, the design looks right, and users can click around normally. Meanwhile: A staging noindex meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header goes to production. robots.txt ships with Disallow: / copied from a preview environment. Canonical tags point at the staging host. A layout refactor wipes page-specific titles and meta descriptions. Routes get renamed with no redirects, so old URLs return 404. A JSON-LD block breaks because someone added a trailing comma. The sitemap still lists URLs that no longer exist. Each of these takes seconds to detect with the right check and weeks to notice from traffic graphs. That gap is exactly what CI is good at closing. The Rule for What to Automate Not every SEO check belongs in a pipeline. Use one simple rule: Automate checks that are deterministic, fast and binary. A tag is present or it isn't. A URL returns 200 or it doesn't. These make good gates. Monitor checks that are noisy or depend on real users. Lab performance scores vary between runs, and Core Web Vitals field data comes from real visitors over weeks. Track these, but don't block merges on them. Keep judgment human. Content quality, search intent, keyword targeting and title copywriting need a person. The Four Layers at a Glance Pull request gate: lint the built HTML for missing or broken tags. Runs in seconds. Lighthouse sample: audit a handful of key templates for SEO and performance budgets. Post-deploy check: test the live server for robots rules, headers, redirects and sitemap health. Scheduled monitoring: catch slow drift such as broken external links and field performance. To decide which individual rules to codify, start from a reference list rather than a blank page. SEO Site Checker's 70 SEO checks explained groups on-page, performance, security and advanced checks with plain-language explanations, which makes it easy to pick the deterministic ones for your linter. Layer 1: Gate Pull Requests on the Built HTML The most important habit is to test the build output, not your source templates. Your framework, your CMS data and your layout components only come together in the final HTML, and that HTML is what search engines see. Point the checks at dist/ , out/ or whatever folder your static export produces. Checks That Belong Here Exactly one non-empty <title> , unique across the site, with a warning above 60 characters A meta description, with a warning above 160 characters A canonical tag that is absolute and points to the production host No noindex in meta robots, except on pages you deliberately allow One <h1> per page (warning only, since some layouts have good reasons) A lang attribute on <html> An alt attribute on every image (an empty alt="" is fine for decorative images) Basic Open Graph tags JSON-LD that parses and includes @context and @type , including inside @graph A Small Checker Script This script uses cheerio to parse every HTML file in the build folder. It separates errors, which fail the build, from warnings, which are only printed. Wire It Into GitHub Actions # .github/workflows/seo-pr.yml name : SEO checks on : pull_request : jobs : seo : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - uses : actions/setup-node@v4 with : node-version : 22 cache : npm - run : npm ci - run : npm run build - name : Lint built HTML run : node scripts/seo-check.mjs dist https://example.com - name : Check internal links uses : lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2 with : args : --offline --no-progress --root-dir "${{ github.workspace }}/dist" "dist/**/*.html" The lychee link checker runs in offline mode here, so it only checks links between your own files. That keeps it fast and immune to third-party sites being slow. External links get checked later, on a schedule. Keep this whole job under about a minute. If an SEO gate becomes the slowest step in CI, people start looking for ways around it. Layer 2: Lighthouse CI on Key Templates, Not Every Page Lighthouse is useful, but it's slow, and its performance scores change from run to run. Running it on every page of every PR is a recipe for flaky builds. Instead, audit three to five representative templates: the homepage, an article, a product or service page and a listing page. Lighthouse CI can serve your static build itself and assert on the results: { "ci" : { "collect" : { "staticDistDir" : "./dist" , "url" : [ "http://localhost/index.html" , "http://localhost/blog/sample-post/index.html" , "http://localhost/pricing/index.html" ], "numberOfRuns" : 3 }, "assert" : { "assertions" : { "categories:seo" : [ "error" , { "minScore" : 0.9 }], "categories:performance" : [ "warn" , { "minScore" : 0.8 }], "largest-contentful-paint" : [ "warn" , { "maxNumericValue" : 2500 }], "cumulative-layout-shift" : [ "warn" , { "maxNumericValue" : 0.1 }] } }, "upload" : { "target" : "filesystem" , "outputDir" : "./lhci-reports" } } } Save that as lighthouserc.json and add one step to the workflow: npx @lhci/cli autorun . Notice the split. The SEO category is an error, because its audits are mostly deterministic (crawlable links, valid hreflang, a document title and so on). Performance is a warning, because CI runners vary in speed. Three runs per URL lets Lighthouse CI use the median result, which smooths out the noise. Layer 3: Check Production Right After Deploy Some of the most damaging problems only exist on the live server. Response headers, robots.txt , redirects and host settings often come from CDN rules, server config or a hosting dashboard rather than your repository. A PR check can't see them, so test production immediately after every deploy. robots.txt and X-Robots-Tag Fail the run if robots.txt blocks everything for User-agent: * , or if key pages send noindex through an X-Robots-Tag header or a meta tag. The header is easy to miss because it never appears in the HTML. Google's robots meta tag and X-Robots-Tag docs explain how both are interpreted. Be precise about Disallow: / . Plenty of sites block specific bots, such as AI crawlers, on purpose, so the check should only fail when the rule applies to every crawler. A Redirect Map Test Keep a redirects.csv file in the repository with two columns, from and to . After each deploy, assert that every old URL returns a single 301 or 308 straight to the expected target, and that the target returns 200. This catches missing redirects, temporary 302s, wrong destinations and chains. Sitemap Sanity Request every URL in the sitemap and expect a 200. Then compare the URL count against a stored baseline, and fail if it drops sharply. A sitemap that suddenly loses a large share of its URLs usually means a routing change or a broken data source, not a deliberate cleanup. If you use a sitemap index, fetch each child sitemap first. Sitemap URLs are checked ten at a time to avoid hammering your own server. Trigger it after a successful production deployment: # .github/workflows/seo-post-deploy.yml name : Post-deploy SEO check on : deployment_status : jobs : smoke : if : github.event.deployment_status.state == 'success' && github.event.deployment.environment == 'production' runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - uses : actions/setup-node@v4 with : node-version : 22 - run : node scripts/post-deploy-check.mjs https://example.com Check what your host calls the production environment. Some platforms report it as Production with a capital P. If you deploy from your own workflow instead, run the script as a final job that depends on the deploy job. Layer 4: Scheduled Monitoring for What CI Can't Judge Some problems develop slowly or depend on things outside your code. Handle them with a scheduled workflow that alerts people instead of failing builds: on : schedule : - cron : " 17 6 * * 1" # Mondays at 06:17 UTC workflow_dispatch : Good candidates for a weekly run: External link checks with lychee in online mode, since other sites change without telling you Core Web Vitals field data from the Chrome UX Report (CrUX) API, which reflects real users rather than a lab run Indexing coverage through the Search Console API, to spot a jump in excluded pages The post-deploy script again, to catch config changes made outside a deploy Post the results to Slack or open a GitHub issue. Nobody should be blocked from merging because a partner's website went down. Automation also doesn't replace a periodic human look at the whole site. Every month or so, run a full SEO audit on your key pages and compare it with the last one. What Not to Automate It's tempting to turn everything into a gate. Resist that for: Content quality and helpfulness. No linter can tell whether a page actually answers the searcher's question. Search intent and keyword choices. These are strategy decisions, not syntax errors. Title copywriting. You can check length automatically, but not whether the title is good. Internal linking strategy. You can check for broken links, but deciding what to link is editorial work. Lighthouse scores on every page as hard gates. They flake, people stop trusting the pipeline, and then they ignore real failures too. Automation keeps the floor up. Humans still have to raise the ceiling. For the judgment side, a manual technical SEO audit checklist covers what a script can't. Rolling It Out Without Annoying Your Team Start with warnings only. Run every check in warning mode for two weeks, fix the existing backlog, then promote the stable checks to errors. Keep an allowlist. Some pages, like internal search results or a 404 page, should be noindex . Put exceptions in one obvious place, like NOINDEX_ALLOWED in the script. Make failures readable. Each message should name the page, the rule and the fix. Consider posting a summary as a sticky PR comment. Give every check an owner. When a rule fires falsely, someone needs to fix the rule rather than add || true to the workflow. Frequently Asked Questions Can you automate SEO testing? Yes, for the technical layer. Anything with a clear pass or fail can be automated: tags, status codes, redirects, robots rules, structured data syntax and sitemap health. Content quality, search intent and strategy still need human review, so automation complements an SEO specialist rather than replacing one. Is Lighthouse enough for SEO checks in CI? No. Lighthouse's SEO category covers useful basics, but it audits one page at a time, doesn't compare titles across pages, can't see your redirects or robots.txt in production, and doesn't validate your structured data against your own rules. Use it as one layer alongside an HTML linter and post-deploy checks. Should SEO checks fail the build or just warn? Fail the build for deterministic, high-impact problems such as noindex on indexable pages, missing titles, broken canonicals and invalid JSON-LD. Warn for things that are noisy or subjective, like performance scores, title length or multiple H1 tags. Start everything as a warning, then promote checks once they've proven reliable. How do I test for noindex and robots.txt mistakes before they reach production? Lint the built HTML for noindex meta tags in every pull request, then run a post-deploy check against production for robots.txt rules and X-Robots-Tag headers. Headers and robots files often come from server or CDN config rather than your code, so the production check is essential. How do I check for broken links in GitHub Actions? Use a link checker such as lychee through its GitHub Action. Run it in offline mode on your build output during pull requests to check internal links quickly, then run it in online mode on a schedule to check external links without blocking merges when a third-party site is down. Do SEO checks slow down a CI pipeline? They don't have to. An HTML linter over a typical static build finishes in seconds. Lighthouse is the slow part, so limit it to a few key templates. Post-deploy and scheduled checks run outside the pull request flow entirely, so they never block developers. Wrapping Up A sensible SEO pipeline has four layers. It gates pull requests on the built HTML, samples key templates with Lighthouse, checks production right after deploy, and monitors slow drift on a schedule. Automate what's binary, monitor what's noisy, and keep judgment human. When you're ready to add your next rule, browse the full list of on-page and technical SEO checks and pick one that your pipeline doesn't cover yet.

title: Webhooks en n8n: evita duplicados al conectar tu CRM
author: Juan Carlos Carpio Cámara
summary: Un formulario envía una consulta. La conexión tarda. El origen repite la entrega y aparecen dos oportunidades en el CRM. Hay otro fallo menos visible: la ejecución termina sin errores, pero durante la transformación desaparece el campo que explicaba qué necesitaba esa persona. Este ejemplo es didáctico. Propone una forma de revisar esas dos situaciones antes de activar una integración. No describe una implantación medida ni una plantilla lista para importar. 1. Define qué entrega estás procesando Empieza por el identificador del evento o envío que proporciona el origen. Combínalo con el sistema y la cuenta de procedencia cuando haga falta para evitar colisiones. Por ejemplo, una clave puede identificar la cuenta, el formulario y el envío envio_001 . Si el proveedor vuelve a entregar ese mismo envío, la clave debe mantenerse. El correo de la persona cumple otra función. Una misma persona puede enviar una consulta hoy y otra distinta mañana. Bloquear cualquier envío que repita correo puede ocultar una petición legítima. Si el origen no ofrece un identificador estable, hay que diseñar esa identificación. Un hash del contenido o una ventana de tiempo son alternativas con compromisos: pueden confundir dos consultas iguales que sí eran independientes. Documenta esa decisión antes de automatizarla. 2. Conserva los campos que importan Escribe una tabla pequeña con tres columnas: campo recibido, campo normalizado y destino. Recibido Normalizado Destino Identificador del envío event_key Registro de procesamiento Correo email Contacto del CRM Motivo de la consulta request_summary Oportunidad o nota Página del formulario entry_page Origen de la consulta El campo de origen puede perderse si el paso de normalización conserva solo nombre y correo. La llamada siguiente puede ser válida aunque la información llegue incompleta. Prueba con valores ficticios que puedas reconocer después. Comprueba el resultado en el registro final, además de mirar los datos recibidos por el webhook. Define qué campos ausentes deben detener el proceso y cuáles pueden quedar vacíos. 3. Registra la recepción antes de darla por aceptada Guarda la clave y un estado de procesamiento en un registro persistente. Para evitar que dos ejecuciones simultáneas acepten la misma entrega como nueva, la exclusión debe aplicarse de forma atómica. Una base de datos con una restricción única sobre la clave es una posibilidad. En PostgreSQL, ON CONFLICT permite decidir qué hacer cuando una inserción encuentra un conflicto. Consultar primero y escribir después, sin protección adicional, deja una carrera entre ambas operaciones. Después, una sola ejecución debe obtener el derecho a procesar el evento. Las demás consultan su estado y no repiten la creación. Si se interrumpe el procesamiento, debe existir una recuperación definida; un estado "procesando" no puede bloquearlo para siempre. Si respondes al origen antes de terminar, hazlo después de guardar de forma duradera lo que has aceptado. En n8n puedes configurar cuándo responde el Webhook. Una respuesta HTTP de recepción y un alta terminada en el CRM son estados diferentes. 4. Resuelve el resultado incierto antes de repetir Imagina que la petición al CRM termina con un timeout. El CRM podría haber creado la oportunidad y haberse perdido la respuesta. Repetir la creación inmediatamente puede duplicarla. Si la API de destino admite claves de idempotencia, utiliza el mecanismo documentado por ese proveedor. No basta con añadir una cabecera que el servidor no reconoce. Si admite una referencia externa consultable, guarda y busca esa referencia para conciliar el resultado antes de volver a escribir. Si no ofrece ninguna de esas garantías, deriva el caso incierto a revisión o diseña otra integración. Un registro local, por sí solo, no garantiza una única escritura en dos sistemas distintos. El estado "completado" debe reflejar un resultado confirmado. Para el resto, distingue error recuperable, resultado incierto y revisión pendiente. Cada uno necesita una salida clara. 5. Prueba las excepciones de forma deliberada Estas son las comprobaciones que usaría antes de activar el flujo. Son resultados esperados, no pruebas ejecutadas sobre este ejemplo. Situación Resultado esperado Entrega nueva y válida Se registra y llega al CRM con todos los campos necesarios Misma entrega repetida Se consulta su estado sin crear otra oportunidad Dos copias simultáneas Solo una obtiene el derecho a procesarla Mismo correo con otro identificador de envío Se evalúa como consulta nueva Timeout después de enviar al CRM Se concilia el resultado antes de repetir la escritura Falta un campo obligatorio Se registra un motivo claro y no se crea un alta incompleta Interrupción tras reservar el evento La recuperación detecta el trabajo pendiente y aplica la política definida Usa datos sintéticos durante estas pruebas. El registro técnico necesita explicar qué pasó, sin copiar por defecto todo el contenido personal del formulario. Del webhook al proceso completo Estas comprobaciones cubren la entrega técnica. title: Securing AI Agents & MCP Servers: OAuth Delegation (XAA) & Exfiltration Detection

summary: Most MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers deployed today rely on static Service Accounts [00:04:14]. title: Building Production-Ready AI Document Understanding Pipelines with GLM-OCR
author: Harpreet Sahota
summary: Document understanding has long been one of the most challenging problems in computer vision. Traditional OCR vision systems excel at character recognition but struggle with complex layouts, tables, formulas, and structured data extraction. Enter GLM-OCR—a lightweight yet powerful multimodal model that's changing how we approach document parsing. In this post, we'll explore what document understanding is and how to build efficient, production-ready AI document understanding pipelines using GLM-OCR integrated with FiftyOne , a powerful dataset management and visualization platform. We'll cover everything from basic text extraction to advanced structured data parsing, with practical document understanding integration examples you can run today. What is document understanding? Document understanding is an AI-powered approach that goes beyond traditional OCR, enabling machines to read, interpret, and extract structured data from documents. By combining vision and language understanding, AI document understanding systems can handle tables, formulas, and layouts, making OCR vision systems smarter and streamlining workflows with seamless document understanding integration. How GLM-OCR differs from traditional OCR vision systems GLM-OCR represents a fundamental shift in how we approach document understanding. To appreciate its value, we need to understand how it differs from traditional OCR vision systems. Traditional OCR vision systems: Character recognition only Classic OCR vision systems like Tesseract, PaddleOCR, or commercial solutions follow a character-by-character recognition approach: Image preprocessing: binarization, noise reduction Text detection: finding text regions Character recognition: identifying individual characters Post-processing: spell checking, language models Limitations: Outputs flat text strings—no understanding of document structure. Struggles with complex layouts (tables become garbled text). Cannot handle formulas (mathematical expressions become meaningless text). Requires extensive post-processing to extract structured data. No semantic understanding—just character patterns. GLM-OCR: Document understanding through multimodal AI GLM-OCR takes a completely different approach. Instead of treating documents as collections of characters, it uses vision-language models to understand documents semantically: Visual-Language Fusion: The CogViT encoder captures both pixel-level details AND layout semantics simultaneously. Contextual Reasoning: Uses language understanding to interpret relationships between text blocks, tables, and figures. Structure-Aware Generation: Generates structured outputs (Markdown, JSON, LaTeX) that preserve document semantics. Multi-Token Prediction: Predicts multiple tokens per step and uses context to correct errors—like semantic proofreading. Key differences: Why GLM-OCR vision systems matters Traditional OCR vision systems give you text, but you still need to parse tables manually or with complex regex, reconstruct formulas from text descriptions, build custom parsers for each document type, and handle edge cases and formatting variations. GLM-OCR gives you semantic structure directly: Tables are already in HTML/Markdown format. Formulas are ready-to-render LaTeX. Structured data matches your exact schema. Document hierarchy is preserved. This fundamentally changes how you build document processing pipelines—from "extract text then parse" to "extract structure directly". Key Advantages: Lightweight: At 0.9B parameters, it runs efficiently on consumer hardware. Multimodal: Handles PDFs and images with equal proficiency. Structure-First: Outputs semantic Markdown, JSON, or LaTeX—not just text. Open Source: Apache-2.0 licensed, deployable anywhere. Context-Aware: Uses language understanding to improve accuracy. The FiftyOne document understanding integration While GLM-OCR is powerful on its own, integrating document understanding with FiftyOne unlocks several key benefits: Efficient Batching: Native support for batched inference, dramatically improving throughput. Dataset Management: Seamless integration with FiftyOne's dataset workflows. Visualization: Built-in tools for exploring OCR results and debugging. Flexibility: Easy switching between operation modes without reloading models. Get started now → Getting started with your document understanding integration Installation First, install the required dependencies. Since GLM-OCR is relatively new, you'll need the latest transformers from source: pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git pip install -U timm fiftyone For the best text viewing experience in FiftyOne, install the Caption Viewer plugin: fiftyone plugins download https://github.com/harpreetsahota204/caption_viewer This plugin provides intelligent formatting for OCR outputs with proper line breaks, table rendering, and JSON pretty-printing—essential for reviewing complex document extractions. Loading your dataset FiftyOne makes it easy to work with document datasets. Let's start with a sample dataset from Hugging Face Hub: import fiftyone as fo from fiftyone.utils.huggingface import load_from_hub dataset = load_from_hub( "Voxel51/scanned_receipts", overwrite=True, persistent=True, name="scanned_receipts", max_samples=50 ) This loads 50 scanned receipt images—perfect for demonstrating GLM-OCR's capabilities. Registering and loading GLM-OCR The FiftyOne integration makes GLM-OCR available as a zoo model: import fiftyone.zoo as foz # Register the model source foz.register_zoo_model_source( "https://github.com/harpreetsahota204/glm_ocr", overwrite=True ) # Load the model model = foz.load_zoo_model("zai-org/GLM-OCR") The model automatically detects and uses the best available device (CUDA, MPS, or CPU), making it easy to get started regardless of your hardware setup. Four operation modes for document understanding GLM-OCR supports four distinct operation modes, each optimized for different use cases: 1. Text recognition The most straightforward mode—extract plain text while preserving formatting: model.operation = "text" dataset.apply_model( model, label_field="text_extraction", batch_size=8, num_workers=2 ) Output: Clean text with preserved layout and structure. Perfect for general OCR tasks where you need readable text output. 2. Formula recognition Extract mathematical formulas in LaTeX format—essential for scientific and technical documents: model.operation = "formula" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="formulas", batch_size=8) Output: LaTeX-formatted mathematical expressions ready for rendering in scientific documents or notebooks. 3. Table recognition Parse complex table structures into HTML or Markdown: model.operation = "table" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="tables", batch_size=8) Output: Properly structured tables in HTML or Markdown format, preserving cell relationships and hierarchies. 4. Custom structured extraction The most powerful mode—extract structured data using custom JSON schema prompts: model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = """请按下列JSON格式输出图中信息: { "company": "", "address": { "street": "", "city": "", "state": "", "zip_code": "" }, "invoice_number": "", "dates": { "purchase_date": "", "purchase_time": "" }, "items": [ {"name": "", "quantity": "", "price": ""} ], "totals": { "purchase_amount": "", "tax_amount": "", "total": "" }, "payment": { "payment": "", "change": "" } } """ dataset.apply_model( model, label_field="structured_extraction", batch_size=8, num_workers=2 ) Output: JSON-formatted structured data matching your exact schema. This is incredibly powerful for building ETL pipelines, data warehouses, or API integrations. Get started now → Real-world document understanding example Let's see GLM-OCR's document understanding in action with a real receipt. After running text extraction, here's what we get: Sarang Hae Yo TRENDYMAX (M) SDN. BHD. Company Reg. No.: (583246-A). P6, Block C, GM Klang Wholesale City, Jalan Kasuarina 1, 41200 Klang, Selangor D.E. Whatsapp : +6012-5060668 www.saranghaeyo.com GST Reg : 000384098304 TAX INVOICE CB#: GM3-46792 15/01/2018 1:48:36 PM Cashier: W001 - erah @ C6 Remarks: Qty Description Price Disc Total 1 MS LOYALTY PACKAGE 15.00 0.00 15.00 SR 10 IB-RDM IRON BASKET ROUND 27 * 25 28.90 -28.90 260.10 SR ... The text extraction preserves the layout beautifully. But with structured extraction, we get machine-readable JSON: { "company": "Sarang Hae Yo", "address": { "street": "P6, Block C, GM Klang Wholesale City, Jalan Kasuarina 1,", "city": "Klang", "state": "Selangor D.E.", "zip_code": "41200" }, "invoice_number": "GM3-46792", "dates": { "purchase_date": "2018-01-15", "purchase_time": "14:36 PM" }, "items": [ { "name": "MS LOYALTY PACKAGE", "quantity": "1", "price": "15.00" }, { "name": "IB-RDM IRON BASKET ROUND 27 * 25", "quantity": "10", "price": "28.90" } ], "totals": { "purchase_amount": "329.10", "tax_amount": "329.10", "total": "329.10" } } This structured output can be directly ingested into databases, analytics systems, or financial software—no manual parsing required. Visualizing results One of FiftyOne's greatest strengths is its visualization capabilities. Launch the app to explore your results: session = fo.launch_app(dataset) Using the caption viewer plugin The caption viewer plugin transforms how you review OCR vision system outputs: Click on any sample to open the modal view Click the + button to add a panel Select " Caption Viewer " from the panel list In the panel menu (☰), select the field you want to view: text_extraction for plain OCR text structured_extraction for JSON outputs Any other text field The plugin automatically: Renders line breaks properly Converts HTML tables to markdown Pretty-prints JSON content Shows character counts This makes it easy to spot issues, verify accuracy, and understand what the model extracted. Performance optimization GLM-OCR vision system delivers impressive throughput: approximately 1.86 pages/second for PDFs and 0.67 images/second. The FiftyOne integration's batching support significantly improves efficiency. Batch size recommendations Choose your batch size based on available hardware: CPU: batch_size=2-4 (slower but works anywhere) GPU (8GB): batch_size=8-16 (good balance) GPU (16GB+): batch_size=16-32 (maximum throughput) Runtime configuration One of the integration's best features is the ability to change operation modes without reloading the model: # Start with text recognition model.operation = "text" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="text") # Switch to table recognition model.operation = "table" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="tables") # Use custom prompt for structured extraction model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = "Extract invoice data as JSON..." dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="invoice_data") You can also adjust generation parameters such as increasing max tokens for longer outputs: # Increase max tokens for longer outputs model.max_new_tokens = 16384 # Adjust batch size for memory constraints model.batch_size = 4 Real-world structured output use cases The true power of GLM-OCR vision systems emerges when you need structured data, not just text. Here are practical use cases where structured extraction is essential, along with how to use the output downstream. Use case 1: Financial document processing Challenge: Extract structured financial data from invoices, receipts, and statements for accounting automation. Why structured output is essential: Financial systems require specific fields (amounts, dates, line items) in exact formats. Flat text requires complex parsing that breaks with format variations. Implementation: model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = """Extract invoice information as JSON: { "vendor": "", "invoice_number": "", "date": "", "due_date": "", "line_items": [ {"description": "", "quantity": "", "unit_price": "", "total": ""} ], "subtotal": "", "tax": "", "total": "", "payment_terms": "" }""" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="invoice_data") Downstream Usage: import json from accounting_system import InvoiceProcessor processor = InvoiceProcessor() for sample in dataset: invoice_json = json.loads(sample.invoice_data) # Direct database insertion invoice_id = processor.create_invoice( vendor=invoice_json["vendor"], invoice_number=invoice_json["invoice_number"], date=invoice_json["date"], total=float(invoice_json["total"]) ) # Add line items for item in invoice_json["line_items"]: processor.add_line_item( invoice_id=invoice_id, description=item["description"], quantity=float(item["quantity"]), unit_price=float(item["unit_price"]) ) # Trigger approval workflow if amount exceeds threshold if float(invoice_json["total"]) > 10000: processor.send_for_approval(invoice_id) Benefits: No manual data entry, automatic categorization, immediate integration with accounting software. Use case 2: Medical record digitization Challenge: Extract structured patient information from scanned medical forms, lab reports, and prescriptions. Why structured output is essential: Healthcare systems require structured data for EHR integration, insurance claims, and clinical decision support. Unstructured text cannot be reliably parsed. Implementation: model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = """Extract patient information from medical document as JSON: { "patient_name": "", "date_of_birth": "", "patient_id": "", "visit_date": "", "vital_signs": { "blood_pressure": "", "heart_rate": "", "temperature": "", "weight": "" }, "diagnosis": [], "medications": [ {"name": "", "dosage": "", "frequency": ""} ], "lab_results": [ {"test_name": "", "value": "", "unit": "", "reference_range": ""} ], "physician": "" }""" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="medical_data") Downstream usage: from hl7 import create_patient_message from ehr_system import EHRClient ehr = EHRClient() for sample in dataset: medical_json = json.loads(sample.medical_data) # Create HL7 message for EHR integration hl7_message = create_patient_message( patient_id=medical_json["patient_id"], name=medical_json["patient_name"], dob=medical_json["date_of_birth"] ) # Send to EHR system ehr.send_message(hl7_message) # Extract and validate lab results for lab in medical_json["lab_results"]: ehr.add_lab_result( patient_id=medical_json["patient_id"], test_name=lab["test_name"], value=float(lab["value"]), unit=lab["unit"], reference_range=lab["reference_range"] ) # Flag abnormal values if not ehr.is_normal_range(lab["value"], lab["reference_range"]): ehr.alert_physician(medical_json["physician"], lab) # Check for drug interactions medications = [m["name"] for m in medical_json["medications"]] interactions = ehr.check_drug_interactions(medications) if interactions: ehr.alert_pharmacist(interactions) Benefits: Automated EHR population, real-time alerts for abnormal values, drug interaction checking, reduced manual data entry errors. Use case 3: Legal document analysis Challenge: Extract structured information from contracts, NDAs, and legal agreements for compliance monitoring and analysis. Why structured output is essential: Legal analysis requires identifying specific clauses, dates, parties, and obligations. These must be structured for automated compliance checking and risk assessment . Implementation: model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = """Extract contract information as JSON: { "parties": [ {"name": "", "role": ""} ], "effective_date": "", "expiration_date": "", "key_clauses": { "termination": "", "liability": "", "confidentiality": "", "payment_terms": "", "governing_law": "" }, "obligations": [ {"party": "", "obligation": "", "deadline": ""} ], "financial_terms": { "amount": "", "currency": "", "payment_schedule": "" }, "renewal_terms": "" }""" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="contract_data") Downstream usage: from contract_analyzer import ContractAnalyzer from compliance_checker import ComplianceChecker analyzer = ContractAnalyzer() compliance = ComplianceChecker() for sample in dataset: contract_json = json.loads(sample.contract_data) # Store in contract management system contract_id = analyzer.store_contract(contract_json) # Check compliance against company policies violations = compliance.check_policy( liability_clause=contract_json["key_clauses"]["liability"], termination_clause=contract_json["key_clauses"]["termination"], payment_terms=contract_json["key_clauses"]["payment_terms"] ) if violations: analyzer.flag_for_review(contract_id, violations) # Extract obligations for tracking for obligation in contract_json["obligations"]: analyzer.create_task( contract_id=contract_id, assigned_to=obligation["party"], description=obligation["obligation"], deadline=obligation["deadline"] ) # Set expiration reminders analyzer.set_expiration_alert( contract_id=contract_id, expiration_date=contract_json["expiration_date"], days_before=90 ) # Generate summary for legal team summary = analyzer.generate_summary(contract_json) analyzer.notify_legal_team(contract_id, summary) Benefits: Automated compliance checking, obligation tracking, expiration monitoring, risk flagging, reduced manual review time. Use case 4: Academic paper processing Challenge: Extract structured metadata, formulas, and references from research papers for knowledge base construction. Why structured output is essential: Academic databases require structured metadata (authors, affiliations, citations). Formulas must be in LaTeX for rendering. References need to be parseable for citation networks. Implementation: # First, extract structured metadata model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = """Extract paper metadata as JSON: { "title": "", "authors": [ {"name": "", "affiliation": "", "email": ""} ], "abstract": "", "keywords": [], "publication_date": "", "journal": "", "doi": "", "references": [ {"title": "", "authors": "", "year": "", "doi": ""} ], "sections": [ {"heading": "", "content": ""} ] }""" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="paper_metadata") # Then extract formulas separately model.operation = "formula" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="formulas") Downstream usage: from knowledge_graph import KnowledgeGraph from citation_network import CitationNetwork from latex_renderer import render_formula kg = KnowledgeGraph() citation_net = CitationNetwork() for sample in dataset: metadata = json.loads(sample.paper_metadata) # Create paper node in knowledge graph paper_id = kg.create_paper( title=metadata["title"], abstract=metadata["abstract"], doi=metadata["doi"], publication_date=metadata["publication_date"] ) # Add authors and affiliations for author in metadata["authors"]: author_id = kg.get_or_create_author(author["name"]) kg.link_author_to_paper(author_id, paper_id) if author["affiliation"]: org_id = kg.get_or_create_organization(author["affiliation"]) kg.link_author_to_org(author_id, org_id) # Build citation network for ref in metadata["references"]: cited_paper_id = citation_net.get_or_create_paper( title=ref["title"], authors=ref["authors"], year=ref["year"] ) citation_net.add_citation(paper_id, cited_paper_id) # Extract and render formulas if sample.formulas: formulas = sample.formulas.split("\n\n") # Assuming formulas separated by double newline for i, formula in enumerate(formulas): rendered_image = render_formula(formula) kg.add_formula(paper_id, formula, rendered_image, position=i) # Extract key concepts from sections for section in metadata["sections"]: concepts = kg.extract_concepts(section["content"]) for concept in concepts: kg.link_paper_to_concept(paper_id, concept) # Generate recommendations based on citation network similar_papers = citation_net.find_similar(paper_id, limit=10) kg.add_recommendations(paper_id, similar_papers) Benefits: Automated knowledge graph construction, citation network analysis, formula rendering, concept extraction, paper recommendations. Use case 5: Supply chain document processing Challenge: Extract structured data from shipping manifests, customs forms, and delivery receipts for logistics automation. Why structured output is essential: Logistics systems require structured data for tracking, customs clearance, and inventory management. Each document type has specific fields that must be extracted accurately. Implementation: model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = """Extract shipping manifest information as JSON: { "shipper": { "name": "", "address": "", "contact": "" }, "consignee": { "name": "", "address": "", "contact": "" }, "shipment_id": "", "tracking_number": "", "ship_date": "", "expected_delivery": "", "items": [ { "description": "", "quantity": "", "weight": "", "value": "", "hs_code": "" } ], "total_weight": "", "total_value": "", "carrier": "", "service_type": "", "special_instructions": "" }""" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="manifest_data") Downstream usage: from logistics_system import LogisticsSystem from customs_api import CustomsAPI from inventory_system import InventorySystem logistics = LogisticsSystem() customs = CustomsAPI() inventory = InventorySystem() for sample in dataset: manifest = json.loads(sample.manifest_data) # Create shipment in logistics system shipment_id = logistics.create_shipment( tracking_number=manifest["tracking_number"], shipper=manifest["shipper"], consignee=manifest["consignee"], carrier=manifest["carrier"], service_type=manifest["service_type"] ) # Submit customs declaration customs_declaration = customs.create_declaration( shipment_id=shipment_id, items=manifest["items"], total_value=float(manifest["total_value"]), total_weight=float(manifest["total_weight"]) ) # Check for restricted items for item in manifest["items"]: if customs.is_restricted(item["hs_code"]): logistics.flag_for_review(shipment_id, item) # Update inventory system inventory.update_in_transit( item_description=item["description"], quantity=int(item["quantity"]), expected_delivery=manifest["expected_delivery"] ) # Calculate shipping costs cost = logistics.calculate_cost( weight=float(manifest["total_weight"]), service_type=manifest["service_type"], destination=manifest["consignee"]["address"] ) logistics.set_cost(shipment_id, cost) # Set up tracking alerts logistics.set_delivery_alerts( shipment_id=shipment_id, consignee_email=manifest["consignee"]["contact"], expected_delivery=manifest["expected_delivery"] ) # Generate shipping labels label = logistics.generate_label(shipment_id) logistics.print_label(shipment_id, label) Benefits: Automated customs processing, real-time tracking, inventory updates, cost calculation, delivery notifications. Multi-mode processing for complex document understanding To understand some documents, they require multiple extraction modes. Here's how to combine them: # Extract text for full-text search model.operation = "text" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="full_text") # Extract tables for data analysis model.operation = "table" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="tables") # Extract formulas for rendering model.operation = "formula" dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="formulas") # Extract structured metadata model.operation = "custom" model.custom_prompt = "Extract key information as JSON..." dataset.apply_model(model, label_field="metadata") Now each document has multiple representations, enabling different downstream uses: Full text: Search and retrieval Tables: Data analysis and visualization Formulas: Rendering in documentation Metadata: Database storage and filtering Quality assurance workflows Use FiftyOne's filtering and evaluation capabilities to build QA workflows: # Filter samples with empty extractions empty_data = dataset.match(F("structured_extraction") == None) print(f"Found {len(empty_data)} samples with no structured extraction") # Review problematic samples session = fo.launch_app(empty_data) # Validate JSON structure import json invalid_json = [] for sample in dataset: if sample.structured_extraction: try: json.loads(sample.structured_extraction) except json.JSONDecodeError: invalid_json.append(sample.id) if invalid_json: print(f"Found {len(invalid_json)} samples with invalid JSON") review_view = dataset.select(invalid_json) session = fo.launch_app(review_view) Architecture deep dive Understanding GLM-OCR's vision system architecture helps optimize your usage: Three-stage pipeline Visual ingestion: CogViT visual encoder captures pixel-level and layout information. Multimodal reasoning: GLM-V-based vision-language fusion aligns visual features with language understanding. Structured generation: Decoder with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) generates structured output while correcting errors. The MTP mechanism is particularly clever—it predicts multiple tokens per step and uses context to fix errors on the fly, acting like semantic proofreading rather than naive character recognition. Batching implementation The FiftyOne integration implements efficient batching through: SupportsGetItem: Custom GetItem transform loads images as PIL Images. TorchModelMixin: Enables DataLoader-based batching. Left padding: Correctly handles decoder-only model generation. Variable-size images: Handles different image sizes in the same batch. This architecture allows processing multiple documents simultaneously while maintaining accuracy. OCR vision system best practices 1. Choose the right operation mode Use text for general OCR and human-readable output Use formula for scientific documents with mathematical expressions Use table when you need structured table data Use custom for domain-specific structured extraction 2. Optimize batch sizes Start with smaller batches and increase until you hit memory limits. Monitor GPU/CPU usage to find the sweet spot. 3. Store raw outputs Always store the raw GLM-OCR output (Markdown/JSON) alongside processed data. This allows reprocessing as your downstream logic evolves. 4. Combine with LLMs GLM-OCR excels at structure extraction. Feed its output into LLMs for: Summarization Question answering Risk analysis Report generation 5. Handle edge cases For low-quality scans, consider preprocessing: Binarization De-skewing Noise reduction This helps the visual encoder and improves structure detection. The future of OCR workflows with AI-powered document understanding GLM-OCR vision systems combined with FiftyOne provides a powerful, flexible solution for AI-powered document understanding. The integration's batching support, visualization capabilities, and multiple operation modes make it suitable for everything from quick prototypes to production pipelines. Key takeaways: Fundamentally different: GLM-OCR understands document semantics, not just characters. Structure-first output: Get Markdown, JSON, and LaTeX directly—no parsing needed. title: GPU Unlock Boosts RTX 30 Series AI Performance by Up to 60%
author: Umar Farooq
summary: GPU Unlock project's published benchmarks show substantial improvements in selected mathematical operations on the RTX 3090 Ti. Results vary by numerical format, demonstrating why the headline performance increase should not be treated as a universal speed boost. The results indicate that the biggest improvements occur in specific compute-intensive operations. They do not mean that every AI application will run nearly twice as fast. Real-World AI Image Generation Gets Up to 60% Faster The most relevant results for everyday AI users come from tests using ComfyUI, a popular interface for image-generation workflows. An RTX 3090 Ti owner reported the following improvements after applying GPU Unlock: MOSS-Image SFT using BF16: 58.6% higher throughput. Qwen-Image 2.1 Turbo using BF16: 57.2% higher throughput. Z-Image Turbo using BF16: 56.1% higher throughput. MOSS-Image SFT using INT8: just 0.3% higher throughput. These results suggest that AI image generation can benefit considerably when its workload relies on the affected tensor operations. However, the tests are community-reported benchmarks on specific hardware and software configurations, rather than guarantees of performance for every user. The minimal INT8 improvement also illustrates an important limitation: workloads using different numerical formats may see little or no benefit. Can GPU Unlock Make Local LLMs Run Faster? GPU Unlock may also improve some large language model (LLM) workloads, particularly prompt processing, where a model evaluates input tokens in parallel. Reported tests using vLLM showed improvements of approximately 33% in prompt processing and inference throughput on an RTX 3090. Other reported results across Ampere GPUs showed improvements of 14% to 36% in LLM prefill performance. However, token generation speed often remains largely unchanged. The reason is that generating tokens one at a time is frequently limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw Tensor Core computing power. Since GPU Unlock does not increase VRAM bandwidth or capacity, it cannot eliminate this bottleneck. For developers running local AI models, the practical benefit will therefore depend on the model architecture, quantization, inference software and workload. Which NVIDIA RTX 30 Series GPUs Are Supported? The project lists support for GPU families GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106, covering a substantial portion of the RTX 30 Series lineup. Potentially compatible models include the RTX 3090 Ti, RTX 3090, RTX 3080 and other Ampere-based cards. However, support is not guaranteed for every board or configuration, and some reported compatibility tests have failed to deliver the expected improvement. The main implementation uses a Linux kernel module that runs before the NVIDIA driver initializes. Because it changes hardware settings during initialization, installation requires more technical knowledge than a typical graphics driver update. An experimental Windows implementation has also been reported, but it uses a different approach and should not be confused with a generally supported Windows release. Does GPU Unlock Improve Gaming Performance? There is currently no convincing evidence that GPU Unlock delivers comparable improvements in gaming frame rates. Although technologies such as NVIDIA DLSS use Tensor Cores, gaming performance depends on many other factors, including graphics workloads, memory bandwidth, CPU performance and the specific instructions used by a game. The reported gains primarily concern AI computing and selected matrix operations. Players should not assume that installing the tool will increase FPS by 60% or improve every DLSS-enabled title. Security Risks and Limitations to Consider GPU Unlock remains an experimental, unofficial modification. Changes to low-level hardware initialization can cause system instability, failed boots, GPU hangs or data corruption, depending on the implementation and hardware. Before considering it, users should: Review the project's source code and installation instructions. Confirm that their exact GPU model is supported. Back up important data and maintain a recovery method. Avoid installing unverified binaries or running commands from untrusted sources. Understand that an unsupported configuration could leave the system unable to boot normally. Users who depend on their computers for production workloads should be particularly cautious. The potential performance gains may not justify the stability risks on a machine that needs to remain reliable. Final Thoughts GPU Unlock could give NVIDIA RTX 30 Series owners a meaningful performance boost for certain AI workloads without purchasing a newer graphics card. Community tests show gains of up to 60% in selected image-generation tasks, while some tensor compute benchmarks improve by considerably more. However, these gains depend on the workload, numerical format and hardware configuration. The project does not increase VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth or gaming performance automatically, and its experimental nature introduces stability risks. For AI developers and enthusiasts running local image-generation models, GPU Unlock is an interesting project to watch. For everyone else, the safest approach is to wait for broader compatibility testing and more independent benchmarks before changing low-level GPU settings.
